name: Indapamide

card.summary: A thiazide-like blood-pressure diuretic with big stroke-prevention trials behind it, but nothing on appearance or depuffing.
card.note: Prescription-only; monitor potassium; interacts with lithium and QT-prolonging drugs.

quick.overview:
Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic prescribed for high blood pressure and for fluid retention in heart failure. It was approved for medical use in 1977.

It is listed in this wiki as a diuretic sometimes grouped with water pills. Its trial evidence concerns blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes, not appearance.
quick.mechanism: It acts mainly on the distal convoluted tubule to increase sodium and water excretion. Its elimination half-life is about 14-18 hours.[1]
quick.risks: Common effects include low potassium, fatigue and dizziness on standing. It should be avoided in sulfonamide hypersensitivity and severe kidney or liver failure, and caution is advised with lithium and QT-prolonging drugs. It is prescription-only.[1]

lead: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic, a prescription medicine that makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water. It is used mainly for high blood pressure and for fluid retention (edema) in congestive heart failure.[1][3] It was patented in 1968, approved for medical use in 1977, and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1]

In looks-related terms, indapamide belongs to the group of water-shedding drugs that appear in conversations about depuffing, because a diuretic reduces extracellular fluid and therefore the water held in tissues. People who discuss it in fitness settings do so mostly as a medication they have been prescribed for blood pressure, asking how it interacts with training or supplements.[20][21] Its effect on facial puffiness or physique leanness has not been the subject of a published trial.

The research base is large but is about cardiovascular medicine: the PROGRESS, ADVANCE and HYVET outcome trials tested indapamide-based regimens, usually combined with the ACE inhibitor perindopril, in stroke survivors, people with type 2 diabetes and adults aged 80 and over.[4][6][5] Newer work includes low-dose triple single-pill combinations that contain indapamide.[10]

paras: Indapamide lowers blood pressure and treats salt and fluid retention in congestive heart failure; the US label lists these two indications.[3] Guidelines place thiazide-like diuretics among first-line antihypertensive options, and a 2022 review noted that thiazide-like agents (chlorthalidone and indapamide) are longer-acting and were the diuretics used in most of the cardiovascular outcome trials that established the benefit of diuretic treatment.[9]
It is also an add-on in resistant hypertension, defined by an American Heart Association statement as blood pressure above goal despite three drug classes that usually include a diuretic.[8]

Diuretics act on extracellular fluid, which is why they come up in discussions of puffiness, bloating and water weight. Indapamide's labelled use for edema in heart failure is a medical setting, and the US label states that routine diuretic use in an otherwise healthy woman is inappropriate.[3] Prescribers decide who receives it, and no published study has tested indapamide for facial depuffing or physique goals.

In monotherapy, indapamide lowers systolic pressure by roughly 10-15 mmHg according to one encyclopedia summary.[2] In the HYVET trial, 3,845 patients aged 80 or older with sustained systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or more were randomised to sustained-release indapamide (with optional perindopril) or placebo; the treated group had fewer strokes at the margin of statistical significance and lower all-cause mortality and heart-failure rates.[5]

PROGRESS enrolled 6,105 people with previous stroke or TIA and tested a perindopril-based regimen with indapamide added at investigator discretion; it reduced recurrent stroke.[4] A PROGRESS substudy reported effects on dementia and cognitive decline and another on white-matter hyperintensities on MRI.[15][16] ADVANCE tested a fixed perindopril-indapamide combination in type 2 diabetes and reported reductions in major vascular outcomes.[6]

Common effects include low potassium, fatigue, dizziness on standing and allergic reactions; potassium, sodium and uric acid are usually monitored.[1][3] The US label warns that severe hyponatremia with hypokalemia has been reported at recommended doses, mainly in elderly women, and appears dose-related.[3]

Contraindications and cautions include sulfonamide hypersensitivity, severe kidney or liver failure, and use with lithium or QT-prolonging drugs.[1][3] Case reports describe photosensitivity with perindopril-indapamide and other unexpected reactions.[13][14] The label notes that diuretics cross the placenta and advises against routine use in pregnancy.[3]

Indapamide inhibits the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, so less sodium and chloride are reabsorbed and more water is excreted.[2] It differs structurally from classic thiazides: an indoline ring replaces the benzothiadiazine ring, making it more lipid-soluble, and it is classed as thiazide-like.[9][2] Its antihypertensive effect is described as dose-related, with diuretic activity more prominent at higher doses.[2]
Indapamide is taken by mouth, is roughly 71-79% protein-bound, is metabolised in the liver and has a half-life of about 14-18 hours, supporting once-daily use.[1]

Indapamide is prescription-only in the UK and EU and appears among diuretics on the WADA prohibited list, which is why athletes consult it.[1] Forum posts that mention it are mostly from people who take it for blood pressure: a T Nation poster asked whether creatine was compatible with indapamide, and another discussed it as a replacement for another blood-pressure drug while tracking heart rate during cardio.[20][21]
In 2025 the FDA approved a triple combination of telmisartan, amlodipine and indapamide (Widaplik) for initial treatment of hypertension, according to one encyclopedia entry.[2]

Registered studies include a phase 4 comparison of indapamide with hydrochlorothiazide in older adults with renal insufficiency (NCT01172431, n=240), comparisons with spironolactone in hypertension, and a planned phase 2 trial in progressive multiple sclerosis (NCT07765212).[7][18][19][17] Fixed-dose triple pills with indapamide were tested in trials published in The Lancet and JAMA in 2024, and a 2026 NEJM trial examined a triple low-dose pill after intracerebral hemorrhage.[10][12][11]

No studies found on indapamide for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Large trials in hypertension, stroke and diabetes include PROGRESS (6,105 participants), ADVANCE and HYVET (3,845 participants), and a registered trial compares it with hydrochlorothiazide in older adults with renal insufficiency.[4][6][5][7]

chain: Blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal tubule
More sodium and water leave in the urine
angle.text: Because indapamide increases urinary sodium and water loss, it is sometimes grouped with other diuretics in discussions of reducing fluid retention. It is prescribed for blood pressure and heart-failure edema, and use for cosmetic depuffing is not a labelled indication.
